This was decreed . . . land: The title likely refers to the invasion of the Viking “great army” under the leadership of Thurkil the Tall in 1009, the year in which the Latin version of 7 Æthelred was composed.

note.seg: Heading in red [not part of the law]

Die Überschrift blickt offenbar historisch zurück, ist also nicht authentisch. Dass sie gerade nur den ersten Däneneinfall meine, ist nicht sicher; wenn das der Fall, begrenzt die Nachricht die Zeit zu eng

The heading evidently looks back historically, and is therefore not authentic. It is not certain that it refers specifically to the first Danish invasion alone; if it does, the statement limits the date too narrowly

Beside the English version in Wulfstan’s style in C.C.C.C., MS. 201, there is a Latin version in Quadripartitus which differs in arrangement and in wording, and has some factual differences. It is more specific on the duties of ecclesiastics and it adds prohibitions, similar to some in previous codes, which are not relevant to the occasion which produced this edict. Two homilies, one by Wulfstan (Napier, No. XXXV) and one a revision of it (No. XXXVI), are closely connected with this edict, but fit any occasion of national calamity, including, besides hostile attacks, famine, murrain, pestilence, etc. The Latin version is sometimes closer to these homilies. It seems likely that different versions of the edict were circulated to various areas. The “Great Army” is probably that mentioned in the Chronicle, 1009. The edict was issued in a year in which Michaelmas fell between Thursday and Sunday, as it did in 992–995, 998–1000, 1004–1006, 1009–1011, and 1015–1016. The more significant variants of the Latin text are given in the notes. Both texts are edited by Liebermann, I, 260–2, and with English translation, by Robertson, pp. 108–16. Thorpe, I, 336–9, has only the Latin version.
